1100.title: Rashi on the Talmud
1100.hook: Rashi explains word by word; without him most learners would be lost
1100.howItsDone: Talmud learners read Rashi's commentary alongside the Gemara, matching each comment's heading words to the line they are studying; in a class, the teacher often reads the Gemara and Rashi together, line by line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the page: the center block, and the columns cupped around it. Your line: the page is a conversation. Today, the inner margin, and the one who explains.

A first-time learner is stuck on one Aramaic word. The line runs on with hardly a pause, and nothing says who is speaking. The page feels like a locked door. A teacher leans over and taps the narrow column at the inside of the page. Start there. Don't read it all. Just find the note on the word you're stuck on. You find it: a few words copied from the text, then a short, plain sentence. The door opens a crack.
screen: `A LOCKED DOOR.` → `START IN THE NARROW COLUMN.` → `ONE WORD AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Rashi on the Talmud. You've heard Rashi's name since year one. It's formed from the initials of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, a teacher in medieval France, in the town of Troyes. He wrote commentary on the Torah and on the Talmud, and his Talmud commentary is the one printed in the inner margin. First, how it works. Each comment opens with a few words copied from the Gemara, a heading, so you can match it to the spot you're stuck on. Then comes a short explanation: what this word means, who is speaking, what the question is. He moves with the text, line by line, rarely stopping to argue. Second, what he does for an argument. Back on the first page of Berakhot, the evening Shema, Rashi pauses on a practice of his own day: people recited the Shema in the synagogue before dark. So how does that fit the mishnah's time? He explains that the evening service is said to stand in prayer out of words of Torah, and that the main duty is fulfilled by the Shema said at bedtime. A short note, and suddenly the text touches a real evening. Third, his own language. Sometimes Rashi glosses a hard word with a word in the French of his day, written in Hebrew letters, so some scholars now read him for old French as well. Some learners say that without Rashi the Talmud would stay closed to them. He doesn't argue with the text. He walks beside you through it.
screen: `A TEACHER IN TROYES.` · `A HEADING, THEN A SHORT NOTE.` · `THE SHEMA BEFORE DARK.` · `OLD FRENCH IN HEBREW LETTERS.` · then, large: `THE GUIDE.`

segments.voice: Picture the narrow column at the inside of the page: a heading, from when, and then the note that the main duty is the Shema at bedtime. Let that land in your own evening, and ask where you end your day. On the breath in, from when; on the breath out, at bedtime.
Rashi on the Talmud. The commentary in the inner margin that explains the Gemara word by word, heading by heading. Today's word.
Your line: the guide. One word explained can open a whole page. One thousand one hundred days now.

1101.title: Tosafot
1101.hook: Rashi's grandsons and their students add questions across the whole Talmud
1101.howItsDone: In a study hall, learners often read a passage of Gemara with Rashi first and then turn to Tosafot, whose questions across tractates are part of advanced Talmud study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rashi on the Talmud: the steady voice in the inner margin, one word at a time. Your line: the guide. Today, the people across the page who asked him hard questions.

A grandfather writes an explanation of the Talmud that his students learn from. His grandsons grow up with it. Then, with their own students, they do something bold. They read his notes next to the Talmud, and next to other pages of the Talmud, and they start asking: does this really fit? What about the place where it says the opposite? Not to tear him down. To finish the work. Their questions end up printed on the outer edge of the page, facing his.
screen: `A GRANDFATHER'S NOTES.` → `THE GRANDSONS ASK: DOES THIS FIT?` → `FACING HIM ACROSS THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Tosafot. Additions. The comments printed on the outer margin of the Talmud page, written by a circle of scholars in France and Germany that began with Rashi's own family. Among them was Rabbeinu Tam, one of Rashi's grandsons, whom you met in year three. First, how they work. Each comment opens like Rashi's, with a heading copied from the Gemara. But where Rashi explains the line in front of you, Tosafot look across the whole Talmud. This page says one thing, but another tractate seems to say the opposite. How can both stand? Then they work out an answer. Second, they ask Rashi too. Back on the first page of Berakhot, Rashi said the evening Shema in synagogue, before dark, is a way to stand in prayer out of words of Torah, and the main duty is the bedtime Shema. Tosafot push back. The bedtime Shema, they note, is said without the blessings that go with the Shema, and for a different purpose. So they bring another explanation, in Rabbeinu Tam's name, that makes room for the early evening practice. A grandson answering his grandfather, on the very first page. Third, the spirit of it. Respect, here, means taking someone seriously enough to question him. Tosafot never erase Rashi. They sit opposite him on the page, and learners read both. Fourth, what that does to a learner. Rashi helps you understand the line. Tosafot make you ask whether you understood it. The page needs both.
screen: `THE OUTER MARGIN: ADDITIONS.` · `ONE PAGE AGAINST ANOTHER.` · `A GRANDSON ANSWERS RASHI.` · `RESPECT MEANS QUESTIONING.` · then, large: `ADDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an explanation you received and never questioned, something a parent said about how the world works, and hold it with respect, the way the grandsons held Rashi. Then ask one gentle Tosafot question: does this fit with everything else I know? You don't have to answer; you're adding, not erasing.

1102.title: The Vilna edition
1102.hook: a printing in Vilna gave the Talmud page an address students everywhere share
1102.howItsDone: Students cite the Talmud by tractate, leaf and side, such as Berakhot 2a, and printed volumes that follow the Vilna layout share that numbering. Some communities study one page a day together in the daf yomi cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tosafot, and your line: additions. Rashi's grandsons and their students, asking hard questions along the outer edge. Today, the page they all sit on.

A message lands in a study group's chat: Berakhot two a, can someone explain the third line? Within minutes three people answer, one at a kitchen table, one on a train, one in a noisy study hall. Their copies were bought in different shops, in different years, maybe in different countries. And every one of them has the same words on the same line of the same page. Nobody had to ask which edition. That quiet agreement has a name and a hometown.
screen: `BERAKHOT 2A, THIRD LINE.` → `THREE ANSWERS, THREE PLACES.` → `THE SAME LINE IN EVERY COPY.`

segments.voice: The Vilna edition. It's the printing of the Babylonian Talmud made in the city of Vilna, and its page became the standard page. First, the address. A Talmud page is cited by tractate, by leaf, and by side. Each leaf has a front, side a, and a back, side b. So Berakhot two a means the tractate Berakhot, the second leaf, the front side. Second, the layout. The Gemara sits in the center, Rashi on the inside, Tosafot on the outside, small notes at the edges. On the Vilna page each of those voices has a fixed seat, and the same words sit in the same seat every time. Third, the numbering. Because later printings copy this page, a reference made in one city lands on the same words in another. That's what lets a whole community study one page together, a page a day, in what's called daf yomi, the daily page. Fourth, a puzzle you met long ago: a tractate's leaves begin with two, not one. Printers' history has its own explanation, and some readers like to add another: there is no first page, because no one ever begins at the very beginning. Someone was always learning before you. Not new words, then, but a shared map.
screen: `TRACTATE, LEAF, SIDE: AN ADDRESS.` · `GEMARA CENTER, RASHI IN, TOSAFOT OUT.` · `ONE PAGE, MANY PRINTINGS.` · `NO PAGE ONE.` · then, large: `THE SAME PAGE EVERYWHERE.`

1103.title: Two Talmuds, one Mishnah
1103.hook: the Jerusalem Talmud, from Galilee, and the Babylonian, built on the same Mishnah
1103.carry: one Mishnah, two Talmuds, both kept
1103.howItsDone: In yeshivas the Babylonian Talmud is the usual text of daily learning, and the Jerusalem Talmud is also studied, especially for the agricultural laws of the land of Israel. Some study cycles move through the Yerushalmi page by page as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vilna edition, and your line: the same page everywhere. Today, a surprise: there is more than one Talmud.

Two families get the same recipe card from a grandmother. One stays in the old house, near the garden where the vegetables on the card actually grow. The other moves far away, to a big city with a busy market. Years pass. Both keep cooking from the card, writing notes in the margins, arguing about the salt. One day the two notebooks are laid side by side: the same card at the center, very different notes around it. That's roughly what happened to the Mishnah. Today's word is the notebook that stayed close to home.
screen: `ONE RECIPE CARD.` → `TWO KITCHENS, FAR APART.` → `TWO NOTEBOOKS.`

segments.voice: Yerushalmi. It's the name for the Jerusalem Talmud, sometimes called the Talmud of the land of Israel. First, a surprise: despite the name, tradition places its sages not in Jerusalem but in the towns of Galilee, in the north of the land. The other Talmud is the Bavli, the Babylonian Talmud, from the academies of Babylonia, far to the east. Both start from the same Mishnah, and both add a Gemara, the discussion, mostly in Aramaic. Second, each shows where it was made. The Yerushalmi discusses the Mishnah's farming laws: the gifts for the poor at the corners of a field, the tithes, the year the land rests. Those laws belong to the soil of the land of Israel, where its sages lived. The Bavli, made far away, gives them much less room. Third, the feel. Some readers who move between them describe the Yerushalmi as shorter and harder, its arguments left more in outline, while the Bavli's run longer and are worked over more. The Talmud this path has been reading, with Rashi and Tosafot around it, is the Bavli. Fourth, the Bavli keeps a hard word about itself. In tractate Sanhedrin, a sage reads a verse from Lamentations about being made to dwell in dark places, and says: that's the Talmud of Babylonia. The Bavli prints that line on its own page, admitting its way of arguing can feel like walking in the dark. Two Talmuds, one Mishnah, and a family that kept both notebooks.

1104.title: Holy unto you
1104.hook: Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre read legal meaning out of the Torah's words
1104.carry: the Sabbath is given to you, not you to it
1104.howItsDone: Students study the Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre alongside the Torah portion or the Talmud, tracing a law back to the verse and the word it was read from. Their teachings are also quoted throughout the Talmud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yerushalmi, and your line: one Mishnah, two Talmuds, both kept. Both grow from the Mishnah. Today, books that grow straight from the verses.

The Torah commands the Sabbath with real force: keep it, don't work, it's holy. It also cares, over and over, about keeping people alive. So what happens on a Sabbath when someone is in danger, and the help they need is work? Rush to them, or rest? A rule book might simply list an exception. The sages wanted more. They wanted to show where in the Torah's own words the answer was already sitting. So they went back to a single verse and read it very, very slowly.
screen: `KEEP THE SABBATH.` → `KEEP PEOPLE ALIVE.` → `WHICH COMES FIRST?`

segments.voice: Law from verses. It's a way of reading where the sages draw practical law out of the Torah's exact words, and a family of books preserves it. First, the books. The Mekhilta reads the book of Exodus. The Sifra reads Leviticus. The Sifre reads Numbers and Deuteronomy. Each walks through long stretches of its Torah book, verse after verse, asking what each word teaches about how to live. Second, how they work. The Mishnah often states a law plainly, with no verse attached. These books do the opposite: they quote a verse, press on one word, and say, from here we learn. Third, the Sabbath question. In Exodus the Torah says of the Sabbath, in the JPS translation, "for it is holy unto you." Unto you. A teaching preserved in the Mekhilta, and in the Talmud too, leans on that small phrase: the Sabbath is handed over to you, and you are not handed over to the Sabbath. So when a life is in danger, the Sabbath gives way. The answer was sitting in one small phrase the whole time; it took a slow reader to find it. Fourth, why it matters. These books show the sages' work in the open: the verse, the word they pressed, the law that came out. Not every reader agrees with every reading, and the books themselves record disagreements. But their claim is quiet and large: the law isn't stacked on top of the Torah. It grows from inside it, word by word.
screen: `MEKHILTA, SIFRA, SIFRE.` · `QUOTE A VERSE, PRESS ONE WORD.` · `HOLY UNTO YOU.` · `THE LAW GROWS FROM INSIDE.` · then, large: `THE SABBATH IS GIVEN TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Take today's phrase, for it is holy unto you, and lean on one word at a time. Holy: what changes when something is holy? Unto: a gift moving toward someone. You: not the Sabbath's servant, but the one it was given to.

1105.title: What Cain said to Abel
1105.hook: Genesis Rabbah and other midrash fill the Torah's silences with stories
1105.carry: midrash listens to the Torah's silences
1105.howItsDone: Jewish readers study midrash collections such as Genesis Rabbah alongside the weekly Torah portion, and teachers draw on its stories when they explain a passage. Rashi's commentary on the Torah also brings some of these midrashim to readers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sages pressed one word until a law came out. Your line: the Sabbath is given to you, not you to it. Today, the same slow reading, but what comes out is a story.

Two brothers. One brings an offering and it's accepted. The other brings one and it isn't. God warns the angry brother that sin is crouching at the door. Then the verse says Cain spoke to Abel his brother, and in the Hebrew, that's where the sentence stops. No words follow. Next, they are in the field, and Cain rises up against Abel and kills him. Something was said, and it ended with a brother dead in a field. The text leaves it blank. The sages leaned into that silence.

segments.voice: Stories in the gaps. You met these brothers long ago; today is about what the sages heard in their silence. It's this path's name for midrash that fills the Torah's silences with stories, and Genesis Rabbah, a collection of midrash on Genesis, is full of them. First, the gap. The Torah tells stories with very few words. It rarely says what people thought, and sometimes, as with Cain, not even what they said. The sages treated those silences as places to stop and listen. Second, what Genesis Rabbah hears. What were they arguing about? It offers more than one answer. In one, the brothers divide the world: one takes the land, the other everything that moves, and soon each is telling the other to get off his property. In another, they argue over whose territory will hold the holy Temple. In another, the quarrel is over a woman. Land, holiness, desire. Third, the midrash doesn't choose. It sets the answers side by side, each a different picture of how brothers come to violence. The silence stays open, now with voices in it. Fourth, a story in the gaps isn't meant to replace the verse. The verse still says what it says, and still stops where it stops. The midrash is a reader saying: here is something this silence might hold, and why it matters to us. Yesterday, that close reading produced a law. Today it produces a story.

1106.title: Why the minority is kept (Mishnah Eduyot 1:5)
1106.hook: minority opinions are recorded so a later court might rely on them
1106.howItsDone: Students of Mishnah and Talmud learn the minority opinions alongside the rulings, and later legal authorities sometimes cite a minority view when a situation calls for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, stories in the gaps: Cain's missing words, and several answers kept side by side. This week went from Rashi and Tosafot to the Vilna page, two Talmuds, and the midrash of law and story. Today, why the losing side stays on the page.

A vote is taken. The motion passes. The sensible next step is to write down the result and move on; in a year, nobody remembers what the no side argued. The Mishnah does something stranger. Page after page, it records the ruling and also the name of the person who disagreed, what he said, and sometimes why. Why keep a losing argument at all? In tractate Eduyot, the Mishnah stops to answer that very question about itself.
screen: `THE MOTION PASSES.` → `THE NO VOTES ARE FORGOTTEN.` → `THE MISHNAH KEEPS THEM.`

segments.voice: Why the minority is kept. It's the Mishnah's own explanation, in Eduyot, of why it records a single opinion that lost. First, the question as it asks it. The law follows the majority. So why mention the words of one person against the many? Second, its answer: so that if a later court sees that lone opinion and agrees with it, that court can rely on it. The minority view is kept on the shelf, not thrown away, with a name attached, for a different time that might need it. Third, the fine print. The Mishnah adds that a court can't overturn the ruling of an earlier court unless it is greater than it, in wisdom and in number. That's a high bar. Some commentators put the two halves together: the minority view was part of the original discussion, so a later court can lean on it without having to overturn anyone. On that reading, the door was left open on purpose. Fourth, another voice, right next to it. The very next mishnah gives Rabbi Yehudah's reason, and it's different: the minority view is recorded so that if someone says, I have a tradition that says this, others can answer: you heard the opinion of that one sage, and the law didn't follow him. One reason keeps the view alive; the other keeps it labeled. And the Mishnah, true to form, keeps both reasons.
